title: Review: Black-body radiation; Compton scattering; Mass defect and binding energy; Fission and reactors; Fusion; Decay law and half-life; Radioactive decay: types and properties; Particles, antiparticles and classification

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Decay constant
items.clue: Symbol λ, unit s⁻¹: the probability per unit time that a nucleus breaks down.

items.label: Fusion
items.clue: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, often with a spare particle.

items.label: Half-life
items.clue: Time for the number of undecayed nuclei of an isotope to fall to 50% of its value.

items.label: Exponential decay law
items.clue: Relation giving the nuclei left after any time t, not only after whole half-lives.

questions.stem: A sample of radon-222 is sealed in a tube. What is the probability that a given nucleus in the original sample has decayed after three half-lives?
questions.explanation: Each half-life, a surviving nucleus has a ½ chance of surviving. Surviving all three: (½)³ = 1/8. So the chance it has decayed is 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

questions.stem: In Compton's experiment, X-rays of a single wavelength were scattered by electrons in a graphite target, and the scattered X-rays were examined. Which observation provides evidence that light is a collection of discrete photons?

options.text: Scattered X-rays had longer wavelengths, by amounts set by the scattering angle
Scattered X-rays had the same wavelength as the incident X-rays at every angle
The wavelength shift was larger when the incident X-rays were more intense
The scattered X-rays traveled more slowly than the incident X-rays did

questions.stem: A gamma-ray photon of wavelength 5.00 × 10⁻¹³ m collides with a free electron that is initially at rest, and the scattered photon moves at 60° to the incident direction. What is the kinetic energy of the electron just after the collision? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.
A student proposes that a free neutron decays into a proton and an electron and nothing else: n → p + e⁻. Which conservation law that holds in all nuclear decays would this proposal break?

options.text: Charge, since two charged particles would come from one neutral particle
Nucleon number, since a neutron would be replaced by a proton
Lepton number, since the number of electrons and neutrinos would rise
Mass, since the proton and electron have less mass than the neutron

questions.stem: A sample contains 8.0 g of a radioactive isotope whose half-life is 5.3 years. What mass of the isotope has decayed after 12 years?

The bar chart shows the total binding energy of each of two nuclei, X and Y, and the total binding energy of the fragments that each nucleus would form by fission. Which claim is supported by the chart?

options.text: Fission of X would need an energy input, since X's fragments have a greater total binding energy than X.
Neither fission would need an energy input, since splitting a nucleus releases energy.
Both fissions would need an energy input, since energy is needed to break a nucleus apart.
Fission of Y would need an energy input, since Y's fragments have less total binding energy than Y.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of nuclear fission?

options.text: Plutonium-239, after taking in a neutron, breaks up into two medium-mass nuclei.
Two hydrogen-2 nuclei join to form a helium-3 nucleus, releasing a neutron and energy.
A uranium-238 nucleus absorbs a neutron and becomes a heavier uranium-239 nucleus.
A water molecule splits apart into two separate hydrogen atoms and a single oxygen atom.

questions.stem: Which statement about the total mass of the particles taking part in fission, fusion and radioactive decay is correct?

options.text: Fission and fusion change the total mass, but radioactive decay leaves the total mass unchanged.
None of the three processes change the total mass, since mass is conserved as in chemical reactions.
Each of the three processes lowers the total mass by converting some of the nucleons into energy.
In each of the three processes the total mass changes, while the total nucleon number stays the same.

questions.stem: Enormous numbers of neutrinos produced by nuclear fusion in the Sun pass through Earth every second, and almost none of them are absorbed or deflected on the way. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: They are uncharged, and uncharged particles pass through matter freely.
Their mass is so small that they slip through the gaps between atoms.
They are long-wavelength electromagnetic waves, which pass through solids.
No electric or strong forces act on them; only the weak force and gravity do.

questions.stem: A photon with energy E, moving in the +x-direction, collides with a free electron that is initially at rest. After the collision, the scattered photon moves in the +y-direction with energy E′. The speed of light is c. Which expression gives the magnitude of the electron's momentum just after the collision?

options.text: √(E²+E′²)/c
E/c

questions.stem: Predict first. A black body is heated to a higher temperature. How does its emission spectrum change?

options.text: It emits more at every wavelength, and the peak moves to a longer wavelength.
It emits more at every wavelength, and its peak moves to a shorter wavelength.
Its peak moves to shorter wavelengths, so it emits less at long wavelengths.
It emits only one wavelength, λ_max, which gets shorter as it gets hotter.

questions.stem: Thorium-232 (²³²₉₀Th) decays through a chain of α and β⁻ decays to stable lead-208 (²⁰⁸₈₂Pb). How many α decays and how many β⁻ decays are there in the chain?

options.text: 4 α and 6 β⁻
12 α and 4 β⁻
6 α and 8 β⁻
6 α and 4 β⁻
